title: The Bamboo-Cutter and the Moon-Child

provenance.tradition: Japanese tale (Taketori Monogatari, The Tale of the Bamboo-Cutter)
provenance.rights: The text is our own retelling of a traditional Japanese tale, Taketori Monogatari, written for Omramo; it does not use the wording of the cited edition. The cited edition is in the US public domain (published before 1931); other territories not verified. Legal review pending (PRD Q23).

geography.lesson: Bamboo groves cover the hills of Japan. The old capital, Heian-kyo, is today’s Kyoto, and Mount Fuji, far to its east, is the highest mountain in the country.

culture.lesson: Bamboo is made into a hundred useful things. At the old court people wrote to each other in five-line poems, and in autumn families still sit out to look at the full moon.

moral.lesson: The lords try to win Kaguya-hime with false gifts and are found out; the Emperor and her father love her truly and still cannot keep her. Loving someone does not make them yours.
moral.reflectionQuestion: The Emperor could have lived for ever. Why do you think he sent the jar up the mountain instead?

moral: You cannot own someone you love, and false gifts are always found out.

cover.alt: At night in a dark bamboo grove, an old man kneels beside a cut stem that glows gold, and a tiny girl sits shining inside it.

card.label: Character · the child from the Moon
card.title: Kaguya-hime
card.body: She was found inside a bamboo stem, no longer than a hand. She is gentle with everyone, and nobody on earth can make her go where she will not.
card.portraitAlt: Kaguya-hime in layered court robes, her long straight black hair loose down her back, with a pale glow around her and a full moon behind.

card.label: Character · her father on earth
card.title: The Bamboo-Cutter
card.body: He has cut bamboo in the same grove all his life. He would bar every door in Japan to keep his daughter beside him, and still he cannot.
card.portraitAlt: The old Bamboo-Cutter in plain hemp work clothes, holding a short cutting knife, with dark bamboo stems behind him and a gold glow on his face.

tapTargets.title: Bamboo work
tapTargets.line: Bamboo is a giant grass with hollow stems that are light, strong and easy to split.

cultureNote.label: From Japan
cultureNote.text: In Japan, people have long split bamboo into thin strips and woven them into baskets, fences and blinds. Flutes, ladles, tea whisks and the handles of writing brushes are made of bamboo too.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A round woven bamboo basket, with a split green bamboo stem and a short cutting knife lying beside it.

tapTargets.title: The old capital
tapTargets.line: A capital is the city where the ruler of a country lives and keeps court.

cultureNote.label: From Japan
cultureNote.text: In the time of this story the Emperor’s capital was Heian-kyo, a city laid out in straight streets like a grid. Today it is called Kyoto, and many of its streets still follow that plan.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A great palace gate with red pillars and a wide tiled roof, at the end of a broad straight avenue under a night sky.

tapTargets.title: Court poem
tapTargets.line: A very short poem of five lines, written with a brush and sent like a letter.

cultureNote.label: From Japan
cultureNote.text: At the old Japanese court, lords and ladies sent each other five-line poems instead of plain letters. A poem was written on fine paper and often tied to a flowering branch.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A folded poem on pale paper tied to a sprig of autumn grass, with a writing brush beside it.

tapTargets.title: Moon-viewing
tapTargets.line: Sitting outside on an autumn evening, simply to look at the full moon.

cultureNote.label: From Japan
cultureNote.text: In Japan this custom is called tsukimi. In autumn families still set out round rice dumplings and tall pampas grass, and sit together to watch the full moon rise.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A small wooden stand piled with round white rice dumplings beside a vase of pampas grass, under a full moon.

paras: ^An old man in Japan once cut bamboo for his living.
From the tall green stems he and his wife made <tap:bamboo-work>baskets and ladles</tap> and flutes to sell, and people called him the <name:bamboo-cutter>Bamboo-Cutter</name>.
One evening, when the grove was already dark, he saw one stem that shone. Light glowed through its green skin like a lamp through paper.
He cut it open with his knife, as gently as he could. In the hollow sat a girl no longer than his hand, looking up at him.
<say:bamboo-cutter*>“I have cut bamboo all my life,”</say> he whispered, <say:bamboo-cutter>“and never found a daughter in it before.”</say>
He carried her home in his sleeve. His wife lined a basket with soft cloth, and there the tiny girl slept.
After that day the old man’s luck changed. Whenever he split a stem of bamboo, gold pieces lay shining inside it.
The child grew as fast as bamboo itself. In three months she was a tall young woman with long black hair, and a pale light came from her. No room she sat in was ever dark.
So she was given the name <name:kaguya>Kaguya-hime</name>, the Shining Princess.
On the blackest night, the old woman could thread her needle at her daughter’s side.
Word of the Shining Princess travelled all the way to the <tap:old-capital>capital</tap>. Soon great lords in ox-carts crowded the lane.
They waited at the fence through rain and snow. One by one they grew cold and went home, until only five were left. Those five would not go.
<say:bamboo-cutter*>“I am old, my child,”</say> said the <name:bamboo-cutter>Bamboo-Cutter</name>. <say:bamboo-cutter>“Choose one of them, so that you are not left alone.”</say>
Kaguya-hime did not wish to marry anyone. <say:kaguya*>“Then let each bring me one thing,”</say> she said, <say:kaguya>“a thing no one has ever brought. I will marry the man who truly does it.”</say>
The first lord had to find a stone bowl that shines by itself. He brought a sooty one from a temple down the road, and it did not shine at all.
The second had to find a branch of gold with jewels for fruit. His looked perfect, until six craftsmen knocked at the door. “Please, lady, he has not paid us for making it!”
The third had to find a robe of fire-rat fur, which no flame can burn. Kaguya-hime laid it on the coals. <pop:1.3>Puff!</pop> It was gone.
The last two lords heard about it and quietly gave up.
Then the Emperor himself came riding to the house among the bamboo.
He saw her shining in the dim room. <say:emperor*>“Come to my palace,”</say> he said. <say:emperor>“You shall be the first lady of the land.”</say>
<say:kaguya*>“I cannot,”</say> said Kaguya-hime. <say:kaguya>“If I am forced, I shall vanish like a shadow.”</say> And already her edges were growing faint.
The Emperor could command anyone in Japan. He looked at her for a long moment, then bowed and rode home alone.
But he sent her a <tap:court-poem>poem</tap>, and she sent one back. For three years their poems flew to and fro like birds.
^In the fourth autumn, Kaguya-hime began to watch the moon.
Night after night she sat on the porch and looked up. It was the season when families sat out to <tap:moon-viewing>admire the moon</tap>, but the rounder it grew, the more she wept.
<say:bamboo-cutter*>“What is it, my child?”</say> asked the old man. <say:bamboo-cutter>“What do you see up there?”</say>
<say:kaguya*>“My first home,”</say> she said. <say:kaguya>“I was not born in this world. I came from the Moon. On the night of the mid-autumn full moon, my people will come to fetch me.”</say>
She held his rough hand in both of hers. <say:kaguya*>“I would stay if I could.”</say>
The Emperor sent two thousand guards with bows. A thousand stood on the roof, and a thousand ringed the wall.
The old man barred every door. He sat in the inmost room with his arms around his daughter. <say:bamboo-cutter*>“Nobody shall take you,”</say> he said.
At midnight the sky turned brighter than ten full moons together. Down from the Moon came a cloud, and on it stood tall, calm people who shone.
The guards lifted their bows, and their arms fell slack. Not one arrow flew. Then, with no hand upon them, the barred doors slid open, <stretch>one after another</stretch>.
<name:kaguya>Kaguya-hime</name> stepped out into the light. She took off her outer robe and put it into her mother’s hands.
<say:kaguya*>“Keep this,”</say> she said. <say:kaguya>“And when the moon is bright, look up. I shall be looking down.”</say>
Then she wrote a letter to the Emperor and set a small jar beside it. Whoever drank from that jar would never die.
A Moon woman held up a robe of feathers. Whoever wore it forgot the sorrows of the earth, and its loves as well.
It settled on her shoulders, and her tears stopped. She stepped onto the cloud, and the cloud rose, grew small, and was gone.
The old couple folded the robe and laid it away. On bright nights they sat on the porch together and looked up.
The letter and the jar were carried to the palace. The Emperor read the letter twice. He did not open the jar.
<say:emperor*>“What use is living for ever,”</say> he said, <say:emperor>“if I never see her again?”</say>
He sat silent for a long time. Then he called his ministers. <say:emperor*>“Tell me,”</say> he said, <say:emperor>“which mountain in my land stands nearest to the sky?”</say>
“There is one in the east, my lord,” they answered, “so high that its head is white with snow.”
So the Emperor’s men carried the letter and the jar up past the trees and past the clouds, to the very top.
There, under the setting moon, they lit a fire. They burned the letter and poured the water of life on the flames, and not one man tasted a drop.
The smoke rose in one thin thread, straight toward the Moon.
That mountain is <tap:fuji-moment>Mount Fuji</tap>. People said the smoke went on rising for many, many years.
And sometimes, on a clear night, a wisp of cloud still trails from its top, like a letter on its way.

landmarks.name: Mount Fuji

low.line: A tall mountain shaped like a cone, with white snow on its top for most of the year.

medium.line: Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan, about 3,776 metres tall.
medium.note: It is a sleeping volcano. It last erupted in 1707, and it has been quiet ever since.

advanced.line: Fuji is a volcano that is resting, not dead: in 1707 its last eruption dropped ash on the city of Edo, now Tokyo.
advanced.note: One old story says the mountain got its name from the smoke in this tale. Nobody knows for certain where the name comes from.

art.alt: A tall, even cone of a mountain with snow on its top, above a lake and low hills, in clear morning light.

sourceNotes: This is our own retelling, written for Omramo, of the old Japanese tale Taketori Monogatari
(The Tale of the Bamboo-Cutter, about 1,100 years old). It is not the wording of any earlier edition.
Documented source for the tale: Yei Theodora Ozaki, "Japanese Fairy Tales" (1908 edition),
"The Bamboo-Cutter and the Moon-Child", Project Gutenberg ebook #4018,
https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4018 (US public domain; other territories not verified).
The source was read for this draft (pglaf mirror, 4018-0.txt) and its phrasing was avoided.
Where our telling departs from Ozaki and follows the wider tradition of the old tale instead:
- Ozaki calls her Princess Moonlight; we use the traditional name Kaguya-hime, glossed in the text
as the Shining Princess. Ozaki has a name-giver name her; we say only that she was given the name.
- Ozaki's old man finds her in the morning and carries her in his hand; ours finds her at dusk
(every scene of this story is dark) and carries her in his sleeve.
- The guards who cannot lift their arms, the robe of feathers that takes away the sorrows of the
earth, the three years of poems, the Emperor's question about the mountain nearest the sky and
his words about living for ever are in the old tale, not in Ozaki, who only says he feared the elixir.
- The sooty bowl is from the old tale; Ozaki's first lord buys a temple bowl that simply gives no light.
- Ozaki sets the coming of the Moon people towards dawn; we say midnight, as the old tale does.
- Our men burn the letter and pour the water of life on the fire; Ozaki's burn it at sunrise.
- Ozaki's Emperor catches hold of her as she flees; ours asks, is refused, bows and rides home.
- The last lines about a wisp of cloud are our own image, not a claim of the source.
Softened for ability age 8 to 10: nobody dies and nobody is hurt; the parting is sad and calm.
Left out: the fourth and fifth tasks (the dragon's jewel and the swallow's shell) and the storm at
sea and the illness that come with them; the second lord's long false story and his beating of the
craftsmen; the court lady sent first by the Emperor; the Moon chief's speech that she was sent to
earth as a punishment; her sip of the elixir; the Buddha as owner of the stone bowl and Mount
Horai as the home of the jewelled branch (kept as plain wonders, no religious content).
Reviewer to check: the name Kaguya-hime and its gloss 'the Shining Princess'; 'Heian-kyo' and the
grid plan of Kyoto; 'tsukimi', rice dumplings and pampas grass; five-line court poems tied to a
branch; ox-drawn carriages for lords; that 'in the east' is right for Fuji seen from the capital;
Fuji facts (3,776 m; last eruption 1707; ash on Edo); the cautious line on the origin of the name.
The mid-autumn full moon is the 15th night of the 8th month of the old calendar (Ozaki: August).
SOURCE CHECK (18 Nov 2026, against Gutenberg #4018 on the mirror): no echo of Ozaki's wording found.
Further departures from Ozaki: her child is three inches tall (ours: no longer than a hand); her bamboo
also yields precious stones; all five of her knights attempt a task (our 'last two gave up' is an
invention, not only a cut); the robe goes to the old man in Ozaki (ours: to the mother); her old man says
he raised the child twenty years (ours: about four); her Emperor comes while hunting; her moon people
ride a flying chariot in the cloud; the baskets, ladles and flutes are ours.
Status: DRAFT. Text review pending. Cultural review (standard: Japanese reader) pending.

palette.mood: Moonlit indigo and bamboo green-black, with silver-gold light that always comes from one source: the stem, the girl, the moon or the fire. Quiet, still and a little sad; never spooky.

artBrief.light: A DARK story: every scene is night or deep dusk, and the words are light on dark. Each picture has one glowing source on the trailing (right) half (the stem, Kaguya-hime, the moon cloud, the pale moon over Fuji); everything else is lit softly from it. Skies are deep indigo, never black, never pale.
world: Japan in the Heian period, about 1,100 years ago. Two worlds meet: plain country people (the old couple) and the Emperor's court.
The grove: tall timber bamboo with clear rings and feathery leaves, stems close together, green-black at night. The glowing stem is lit from inside, gold through green, like a paper lamp.
The old man's tools: a short, broad cutting knife or hatchet (nata) with a wooden handle, a carrying cord, finished baskets, ladles and a flute. No saw, no long sword.

The house: wooden posts, plank and earth walls, a thick thatched roof, a narrow raised wooden porch, a simple woven bamboo fence. After the gold it is larger and neater but still a thatched country house, not a palace.

The old couple wear plain undyed or dull blue hemp work clothes: a short wrapped jacket tied with a cloth cord, narrow trousers or leggings, straw sandals. The old man's white hair is tied in a small knot; the old woman's grey hair is tied back low.

Kaguya-hime wears Heian court dress: many thin robes one over another, showing as coloured bands at the neck and sleeves, very wide sleeves, long trailing hems. Her black hair is very long and perfectly straight, loose down her back to the floor, with no pins or ornaments.
Court men (the lords, the Emperor, the ministers) wear wide-sleeved robes with full trousers and a tall black lacquered cap. The Emperor's robe is the richest but plain in shape; no crown.
The lords travel in ox-drawn carriages: a boxed two-wheeled cart with large wheels and a curved roof, pulled by one ox, with an ox-boy. The Emperor rides a horse with a simple saddle.
The guards are Heian archers: long bows held upright, quivers on the back, plain robes and caps or simple early armour of laced plates. They look helpless and astonished, not fierce.

The Moon people are tall, calm, robed figures standing on a low bank of shining cloud, drawn in pale silver-gold with little detail. The robe of feathers is a long light mantle of pale feathers. No wings, no halos.
The jar is a small plain lidded jar that fits in one hand. The letter is a folded sheet of pale paper. The poems are folded papers, sometimes tied to a sprig.
Mount Fuji as people of that time knew it: an even cone with snow on its head and a thin thread of smoke from the top (it was an active volcano then). Seen from far off across dark hills.

Avoid: samurai armour and katana of later centuries, castles, geisha, kimono with a wide obi sash (a later fashion), parasols, paper lanterns everywhere, cherry blossom everywhere, torii gates, pagodas, a rabbit in the moon, winged angels, spaceships. Avoid slanted-eye caricature; draw each person as a particular, dignified person.

characters.kaguya: A slim young woman, about three heads tall, with a calm oval face and small plain eyes. Layered court robes in pale gold over soft white and moon-blue; black hair straight to the floor. Signature detail: a soft pale glow around her that lights whatever is near. On page 1 she is a tiny child no longer than a hand, sitting in the hollow stem.
characters.bamboo-cutter: A small, thin, weathered old man with a white topknot, wispy white beard and kind creased eyes. Dull blue-grey hemp jacket and leggings, straw sandals. Signature details: the short cutting knife at his belt, and big careful hands.
characters.emperor: A young man with a grave, gentle face, in a wide-sleeved robe of deep purple and a tall black court cap. Signature detail: he holds a folded letter. Dignified and sad, never angry.

scene-grove.unfolded: Night. Far: an indigo sky with a few stars seen between bamboo tops. Middle: ranks of dark bamboo stems, densest on the trailing (right) half. Near, on the right: the Bamboo-Cutter bending with his knife towards one stem that glows gold from inside, the glow lighting his face and the nearest stems. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are calm dark indigo sky above low dark leaves.
scene-grove.folded: The glowing stem cut open in the middle of the band, the tiny girl sitting in the hollow, and the old man's gold-lit face leaning in beside it; dark stems around, dark sky above for the words.

scene-house.unfolded: Deep dusk, sky dark indigo with a last dull violet low down. Far: black bamboo tops. Middle, on the trailing (right) half: the thatched house with pale silver-gold light pouring from its open doors and through the cracks, as if a moon were inside. Near: a woven bamboo fence with two ox-carts and a few waiting lords in tall black caps, small and dark against the light. The leading pane's upper two thirds are calm dark sky.
scene-house.folded: Kaguya-hime sitting in the doorway in the middle of the band, her long hair down her back, her own glow lighting the door posts and the porch; dark sky above.

scene-moon.unfolded: Night of the full moon, sky deep blue. Far, upper right: a huge full moon. Middle: a low bank of shining cloud gliding down from it with five or six tall, calm robed figures. Near, on the trailing (right) half: the roof and wall of the house lined with archers whose bows hang slack, and the doors standing open. The leading pane's upper two thirds are open deep-blue sky with a few stars.
scene-moon.folded: The shining cloud and its tall figures in the middle of the band with the great moon behind them, and a line of small dark archers on the roof ridge below.

scene-fuji.unfolded: Deep blue before dawn. Far, on the trailing (right) half: the great even cone of Mount Fuji with snow on its head and one thin thread of smoke rising straight up towards a pale moon. Middle: dark layered hills and a band of low cloud. Near: tiny figures with one small torch climbing the lower slope. The leading pane's upper two thirds are calm deep-blue sky.
scene-fuji.folded: The snowy top of Fuji in the middle of the band, the thin thread of smoke rising from it to a pale moon above, dark hills below.

pictures.bamboo-work: One round woven bamboo basket in the centre, with a split green bamboo stem and the short cutting knife lying in front of it, on a deep green ground.
pictures.old-capital: One great palace gate seen from the front: red pillars, white walls, a wide roof of dark tiles with gently upturned ends, at the end of a broad straight avenue, under a night sky.
pictures.court-poem: One folded poem on pale paper tied with a thin cord to a sprig of autumn grass, with a writing brush lying beside it, on deep indigo.
pictures.moon-viewing: One small plain wooden stand with a neat pile of round white rice dumplings, a vase of feathery pampas grass beside it, and a full moon above.

portraits.kaguya: Half figure, turned a little towards a full moon behind her shoulder; layered pale robes, long straight black hair, a soft glow round her; calm and a little sad. Deep indigo behind.
portraits.bamboo-cutter: Half figure in his hemp jacket, holding his short knife low, looking down in wonder with a gold light on his face from below; dark bamboo stems behind.

artBrief.cover: Night in the grove: the old Bamboo-Cutter kneeling beside the one cut stem that glows gold, the tiny girl sitting inside it looking up at him, in the middle of the picture; dark bamboo and indigo sky all round.

landmarks.mount-fuji: Our own drawing of Mount Fuji by day, as it looks now: a tall, even cone with snow on its top, above a lake and low wooded hills, in clear morning light. No smoke (the volcano is quiet today). No photograph traced.
